figures.caption: Figure 1 Annual publication counts of academic papers related to batteries that mention quantum- mechanics (QM) based calculations (blue) and machine-learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs; orange). Publications from 1990 to 2025 were surveyed using the Scopus database. The quantum mechanics-based calculations search used ("first-principles calculations" OR "ab initio calculations") AND ("battery" OR "batteries"), whereas the MLIP-related search used the query ("neural network potential" OR "machine learning interatomic potential") AND ("battery" OR "batteries") (search performed in March 2026). The reported counts should be regarded as a qualitative indicator of publication trends, since they include papers that mention these keywords and are not necessarily original studies primarily focused on applying these methods to battery materials.

Figure 2 (a) Schematic illustration of representative bulk reaction modes in battery electrode materials. Upon insertion and extraction of guest ions, the host framework remain unchanged, as in intercalation reactions, or undergo substantial structural reorganization, as in conversion, alloying, and amorphization reactions. For such bulk processes, MLIPs are expected to serve as a powerful tool for understanding (i) ion diffusion in bulk and reaction phases, as well as (ii) phase stability in reaction and product phases, including defects, order/disorder ion arrangements, and so on. (b) Schematic illustration of electrode/electrolyte interfacial processes in battery materials. Figure 3 Classification of current MLIPs. Hand-crafted descriptor–based methods are categorized as Category A, and Learned descriptors–based methods as Category B. Furthermore, based on the type of machine learning approach used, Category A is subdivided into A1–A3 and Category B into B1– B2. Underlined terms indicate representative software.

Figure 4 Conceptual diagrams related to hand-crafted descriptors. (a) A general MLIP scheme for evaluating energy using hand-crafted descriptors. The atomic position vectors 𝑅𝑖 are transformed into symmetry functions 𝐺𝑖 that are invariant with respect to translation, rotation, and permutation of identical atoms. These symmetry functions are defined for each atom as descriptors representing the local environment around that atom, and the atomic energy 𝐸𝑖 is evaluated through the corresponding subnetwork 𝑆𝑖 for each element type. The total energy of the system 𝐸 is given as the sum of the atomic energies. Reprinted from the paper12 with permission of APS. Figure 5 Examples of MLIP architectures based on learnable descriptors. (a) (upper) Conceptual illustration of crystal-structure representation in a graph neural network. Atoms are treated as nodes with atomic features, while neighboring atom pairs within a cutoff radius are connected as edges with interatomic information as edge features. (lower) Example of property prediction in a non-equivariant graph neural network (CGCNN). After graph construction, message passing updates atomic features, and pooling generates a whole-structure representation for predicting the target property115. Reprinted from the paper115 with permission of APS. (b) Specific example of message passing (MEGNet). First, each edge descriptor is updated using the connected node descriptors and its own features as input.
